extracted.intended_audience: journalists, editors, media critics, and readers interested in press criticism and newsroom strategy
extracted.subtask_description: A practitioner rubric for selecting and elevating journalism stories in the platform era, emphasizing how stories change the political-economic conditions of news production and distribution. Used by critics/editors to decide which platform-, labor-, legal-, and business-related developments merit sustained coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform leverage stories
rubrics_metrics.description: How Meta / Google / X squeeze publishers
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize reporting that reveals how major platforms extract value from or disadvantage publishers — e.g., algorithm or policy changes that reduce referral traffic, monetization shifts, preferential treatment of platform-native content. Examples: platform algorithm/policy changes that throttle news; coverage should show concrete mechanisms of leverage and their effect on journalism revenue or reach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subscription / membership model dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: Coverage of how subscription or membership strategies are evolving and affecting the sustainability of news organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include stories about paywall strategies, membership experiments, conversion and retention metrics, and their implications for newsroom independence and business viability. Evaluate whether changes signal broader shifts in the economics of journalism rather than isolated product moves.

rubrics_metrics.name: AI implications for journalism business
rubrics_metrics.description: How artificial intelligence affects journalism's business models, labor, distribution, and legal exposure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elevate stories that analyze AI's impact on content creation, monetization, training-data lawsuits, and workflow/tooling changes. Distinguish substantive, structural consequences (e.g., police of training data, automation of reporting tasks) from hype about superficial applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsroom labor and editorial-independence tensions
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories about labor actions, unionization, layoffs, and conflicts between editorial independence and commercial/management pressures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize coverage of labor actions at major publishers and cases where newsroom editorial decisions are constrained by ownership or commercial interests. Look for implications for reporting quality, independence, and long-term institutional health.

rubrics_metrics.name: International press-freedom incidents
rubrics_metrics.description: Incidents abroad that threaten press freedom, censorship, or journalists' safety and legal rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report on arrests, legislative changes, government clampdowns, or transnational legal cases that alter journalists' ability to report. Note cross-border consequences for global news operations and precedents that could be emulated elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open-web vs. walled-garden battles
rubrics_metrics.description: Conflicts between open-web principles and platform/closed-garden strategies that shape access to news and link culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cover policy, product, and business developments that favor walled gardens (e.g., platform-hosted news hubs, reduced linking) over an open web, and analyze long-term effects on discoverability, attribution, and independent publishers.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Does this story affect the structural conditions of journalism?"
rubrics_metrics.description: "Does this story affect the structural conditions of journalism?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as a primary test: prefer stories that change the underlying political-economic environment (business models, distribution infrastructure, legal regimes) rather than purely episodic events. Ask what systemic levers are altered.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Is there a power asymmetry being exposed?"
rubrics_metrics.description: "Is there a power asymmetry being exposed?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize stories that reveal imbalances (platforms vs. publishers, owners vs. journalists, states vs. press) and the mechanisms of that imbalance. Coverage should illuminate who holds leverage and how it is exercised.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Are publishers / journalists acting as a class on this?"
rubrics_metrics.description: "Are publishers / journalists acting as a class on this?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elevate stories showing collective action or coordinated responses (industry coalitions, union drives, coordinated legal strategies), as these indicate sector-level change rather than isolated incidents.

rubrics_metrics.name: "What's the long-arc consequence?"
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider longitudinal impact: will this development reshape journalism over years? Favor reporting that links short-term events to longer-term trends and structural outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform algorithm / policy changes that throttle news
rubrics_metrics.description: Platform algorithm or policy changes that reduce distribution, visibility, or monetization for news publishers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat these as high-priority stories; explain the specific policy/algorithm change, its measurable impact on traffic/revenue, and potential remedies or industry responses. Use data where possible to demonstrate effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labor actions at major publishers
rubrics_metrics.description: Strikes, unionization efforts, layoffs, and other labor actions within large news organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elevate coverage of labor movements that signal broader pressures on the industry (cost-cutting, changing labor models). Connect labor stories to editorial outcomes and business strategy where relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lawsuits over journalism (training data, anti-SLAPP, defamation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Legal cases that affect journalistic practice, liability, or the business (e.g., AI training-data suits, anti‑SLAPP rulings, defamation suits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on litigation that sets precedents or imposes costs/constraints on reporting. Explain legal issues, potential chilling effects, and sector-wide implications rather than treating suits as isolated disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding mechanism experiments (NewsMatch, foundation models)
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiments and new models for funding journalism, including philanthropy-led initiatives and technological/platform-based funding approaches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report on whether these mechanisms materially change sustainability prospects for newsrooms, who they benefit, and any strings/conditions that might affect editorial independence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tech press hype
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories driven by hype from the tech press rather than substantive structural importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demote coverage that merely repeats vendor/PR-driven claims or transient excitement without demonstrating long-term consequences. Avoid amplifying superficial product announcements unless they meaningfully alter journalistic practice or economics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Performative outrage about minor controversies
rubrics_metrics.description: Coverage that centers performative outrage over small or local disputes lacking systemic significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deprioritize stories that are mainly performative or attention-seeking and do not reveal broader structural problems. Reserve space for controversies that have demonstrable institutional or policy implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Personality-driven media gossip
rubrics_metrics.description: Gossip and personality-focused coverage that centers individuals rather than systemic issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid elevating personality-driven narratives unless they illuminate institutional dynamics, conflicts of interest, or patterns with wider relevance to journalism's functioning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overall rubric — structural test for newsworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Ingram's rubric is structural — newsworthy = changes the political-economic terrain on which journalism operates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame editorial selection around structural impact: ask whether a story alters incentives, power relations, legal/regulatory frameworks, or funding/distribution systems for journalism. Use the Tests (structural effect, power asymmetry, collective action, long-arc consequence) together to assess stories.
